title: Lesson 75: Agent Architecture Patterns: Orchestration, Planning, and Tool Use
description: The three capabilities that turn a language model into an agent: tool use, orchestration (single vs multi agent), and planning. It covers the workflow-versus-agent distinction, the agent-computer interface, the orchestrator-worker pattern, plan-and-execute, and the token cost of each architectural choice.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the single load-bearing difference between a workflow and an agent?
options: A workflow is fixed code paths orchestrating LLMs and tools, while an agent lets the LLM dynamically direct its own process and tool usage.
A workflow uses many models while an agent uses one model.
A workflow never calls tools while an agent always does.
A workflow runs on a server while an agent runs on a client device.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's distinction is that a workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths, while an agent lets the LLM dynamically direct its own process and tool usage, maintaining control over how it accomplishes the task.

questions.question: A team is building an agent that needs to research a service failure that could have several independent root causes. The plan-and-execute approach is chosen. What best describes what happens when one executor returns an unexpected result?
options: The system immediately stops and returns an error to the user.
The planner is called again with a re-planning prompt to decide whether to finish or generate a follow-up plan.
Every executor re-runs its tool calls from scratch in a new context window.
The orchestration moves from a single agent to a workflow with fixed code paths.
questions.explanation: In plan-and-execute, once execution completes, the agent is called again with a re-planning prompt that lets it decide whether to finish with a response or generate a follow-up plan when the first plan did not have the desired effect.

questions.question: A client asks to scale its research agent into a multi-agent orchestrator-worker system. Using the lesson's token accounting, what should the architect weigh before committing?
options: Multi-agent systems use about 15x more tokens than chats, so the added capability must earn the increased spend.
Single-agent systems always use more tokens than multi-agent systems.
Tokens are the same regardless of the number of agents.
Multi-agent systems reduce token use because subagents share one context window.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's data shows agents use about 4x more tokens than chat while multi-agent systems use about 15x more than chats, so multi-agent architectures require tasks with high enough value to pay for the increased performance.
